title: Canary-Controlled Safe-Data Interleaving for Reducing Emergent Misalignment

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to mitigate emergent misalignment (EM) during fine-tuning by dynamically adjusting defense strength based on the model's real-time risk state, rather than using fixed interleaving ratios. Several prior papers address emergent misalignment, but none propose a dynamic, risk-state-based adjustment mechanism. For example, [1], [2], [5], and [7] discuss emergent misalignment and its mitigation, but they focus on static or mechanistic approaches (e.g., latent blocking in [2] or unlearning in [5]) rather than dynamic, real-time adjustments. No prior paper explicitly shares the purpose of dynamically adapting defense strength to the model's risk state.

### Mechanism
The mechanism is a closed-loop, canary-controlled adaptive interleaving framework that evaluates canary prompts during training, computes an EMA-smoothed risk estimate, and adjusts the safe-data interleaving ratio via a threshold-based policy with hysteresis. While [13] and [15] describe interleaving-based control frameworks, they are in unrelated domains (vehicle stability and optimal control) and do not involve canary prompts, risk estimation, or hysteresis policies. Similarly, [16] uses canaries for exploitability evaluation, but this is unrelated to adaptive interleaving or fine-tuning alignment. No prior paper combines these elements into a substantively equivalent mechanism.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses the Security EM benchmark with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, achieving a 25% relative improvement in General %Misaligned compared to fixed interleaving. While the specific benchmark instance (Security EM) and model (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) are new, the evaluation design — measuring misalignment reduction on a benchmark with a fixed metric — is not novel. For example, [1], [2], [5], and [10] all evaluate misalignment mitigation using similar benchmark-based designs, even if the specific benchmarks or models differ. Thus, the evaluation design is covered.

### Domain
The domain is LLM safety and fine-tuning alignment. This is a well-established area, with numerous prior papers ([1], [2], [5], [7], [8], [9], etc.) addressing emergent misalignment and safety in fine-tuning. While this contribution targets a specific sub-problem (dynamic risk-based adjustment), it remains within the broader domain of LLM safety and alignment.
